stories.title: Nvidia Bets Its Balance Sheet on OpenAI's Ohio Megacampus
stories.story:
The numbers alone are staggering, but the structure of the deal is what makes it historic. Nvidia is in talks to provide roughly $250 billion in financing guarantees so that OpenAI can lease a 10-gigawatt data center campus being built on a decommissioned uranium-enrichment site in southern Ohio — a project whose total cost, including chips, could exceed $500 billion, making it the largest AI infrastructure commitment ever announced.

The mechanism matters as much as the magnitude. OpenAI has no investment-grade credit rating and remains unprofitable despite 900 million weekly active users. Banks won't lend against OpenAI's balance sheet. But they will lend against Nvidia's. So the proposal is essentially a co-signature: Nvidia backstops the lease, SoftBank's energy subsidiary builds the campus, and Japan funds the 9.2 gigawatts of new natural-gas generation required to power it — money committed under a trade deal with Washington. Separately, Nvidia is negotiating another $350 billion arrangement to finance OpenAI's chip purchases from Nvidia itself.

The conflict of interest is almost elegant in its circularity: Nvidia guarantees the building so OpenAI can afford to buy the chips that Nvidia sells, cementing demand for years. For OpenAI, the prize is independence — this would be the first time it controls its own infrastructure rather than renting compute from Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick controls power allocation at the site, and Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google have all lobbied him for access.

What this implies is a fundamental restructuring of who underwrites AI at scale. Chip companies are becoming the silent lenders of the intelligence economy — not just suppliers, but creditors whose financial exposure now rivals that of sovereign wealth funds.
stories.hook: Nvidia isn't just selling the shovels in the AI gold rush — it's now co-signing the mortgage on the mine.

stories.title: An AI Broke a Post-Quantum Cipher in 60 Hours Flat
stories.story:
For two years, cryptographers around the world — vetted by NIST, the U.S. government's standards body — combed through HAWK, a digital signature scheme designed to survive quantum computers. They found nothing fatal. Then Anthropic pointed its unreleased Claude Mythos Preview at the same problem and gave it a long weekend.

In roughly 60 hours, the model independently found a previously unknown flaw in HAWK-256, exploiting an unused symmetry in the lattice structure behind the scheme. The attack reduced the work required to recover a signing key from approximately 2^64 operations to 2^38 — about 67 million times less effort — for a compute bill of around $100,000. The model also invented a separate technique, which it named the Möbius Bridge, that makes an existing attack on a weakened version of AES run 200 to 800 times faster.

The caveats matter: HAWK has never been deployed anywhere, and the AES result targets a seven-round research variant, not the full cipher protecting your bank. No production system is at immediate risk. But those caveats miss the point that specialists are focused on: the pace. NIST's peer-review process is measured in years and staffed by some of the best mathematicians alive. A frontier AI matched and exceeded it in days, largely autonomously, for the cost of a mid-size marketing campaign.

The structural implication is uncomfortable. If a $100,000 compute run can stress-test a NIST finalist, any well-funded actor — and not just nation-states — can now run cryptanalysis campaigns that were previously available only to the largest intelligence agencies. The window between a cipher's publication and its vulnerability to AI-assisted attack has just gotten shorter in ways that nobody has yet had time to fully quantify.
stories.hook: We used to assume cryptography was safe until quantum computers arrived — it turns out we also have to worry about a three-day AI weekend.
stories.source: Anthropic Research Blog / The Hacker News, July 28–29, 2026

stories.title: Azure Crosses $100 Billion, Settling the AI Returns Debate
stories.story:
For most of this fiscal year, Microsoft was the cautionary tale of the AI boom: a company pouring tens of billions into data centers while its stock shed nearly 20% as investors demanded proof that the spending would ever pay off. On Wednesday evening, it delivered that proof in a single earnings report.

Microsoft posted fourth-quarter revenue of $90 billion, up 18% from a year ago, handily beating the $87.6 billion Wall Street had expected. The headline number mattered less than what was inside it. Azure cloud growth accelerated to 43% — three points above guidance — and for the full fiscal year, Azure crossed $100 billion in revenue for the first time. Microsoft 365 Copilot, the AI assistant embedded across Office products, now has over 30 million paid seats, with net additions doubling quarter-over-quarter as enterprise customers moved into premium tiers. Contracted future revenue — work already sold but not yet billed — jumped 84% to $678 billion, a figure that turns the AI investment argument from speculation into an order book.

The market's reaction was visceral. Microsoft surged 15.5% on Thursday, the largest single-day gain in absolute market-value terms in stock market history, adding roughly $450 billion to its capitalization in one session. The Nasdaq followed, posting its best day in weeks.

The deeper significance is structural. Microsoft spent $145 billion in capital expenditures this fiscal year and is guiding toward more than $50 billion per quarter going forward. It is simultaneously extending the accounting life of its data centers from 15 to 25 years — a quiet move that reduces future depreciation charges and signals management's conviction that this infrastructure will generate returns for decades, not quarters. The question the market has been asking — when does AI spending become AI revenue? — now has a concrete, audited answer.
stories.hook: The AI investment thesis just graduated from faith to financials.
stories.source: Microsoft Q4 FY2026 earnings release; Quartz; Axios

stories.title: Amazon Crosses $200 Billion in a Quarter, AWS Accelerates Again
stories.story:
For two years, the central anxiety about Big Tech's AI spending binge was simple: where is the revenue? Amazon answered that question Thursday night in a single data point. AWS grew 37% in Q2 2026 — its fastest pace in 18 quarters — generating $42.2 billion in cloud revenue against analyst expectations of $40.5 billion. Crucially, the growth rate accelerated from 28% just one quarter ago, suggesting demand is pulling forward, not plateauing.

The headline number was equally striking. Total Amazon revenue crossed $200 billion in a single quarter for the first time, reaching $200.6 billion. Operating income rose 43% to $27.5 billion, and AWS alone contributed $16.6 billion of that — a 39.4% operating margin that bested even Google Cloud's 35.6%. Andy Jassy disclosed that AWS's contracted backlog now stands at $496 billion, a figure that functions less as a forecast than as a statement of structural lock-in.

The cost of that position is not trivial. Capital expenditures on a trailing twelve-month basis hit $169 billion, up 64% year-over-year. Jassy raised full-year capex guidance to $220 billion, a number that has tipped free cash flow into negative territory. The mechanism here is the same across every hyperscaler: AI workloads are so computationally hungry that capacity is being signed up faster than it can be built, creating a multi-year demand floor for chips, power, and fiber.

What comes next is a competition less about cloud features than physical infrastructure. AWS's AI and custom-chip businesses each now run at $25 billion annualized rates, both more than doubling year-over-year. The company that builds the most data center capacity, fastest, is likely to lock in the enterprise AI contracts of the next decade — which is exactly why the $220 billion number is not an expense. It is a land grab.
stories.hook: When your backlog hits half a trillion dollars, the question isn't whether AI spending is working — it's whether anyone can catch up.

stories.title: Blackstone Buys HSBC's $25 Billion Australian Mortgage Book
stories.story:
For most of its history, a mortgage was a bank's most prized asset: a long, steady stream of interest payments sitting on the balance sheet. Today HSBC announced it is handing that stream — A$36 billion, or roughly $25 billion, of Australian home and personal loans — to Blackstone, the private equity and credit giant, in what Blackstone itself called the largest home loan portfolio transaction ever completed globally.

The logic runs in both directions. HSBC's new CEO Georges Elhedery has spent nearly two years stripping the bank back to what he calls its East-West corridor: trade finance, wholesale banking, and wealthy Asian clients. Australia's retail mortgage book, with its thin margins and the capital charges Basel rules impose on consumer loans, was a misfit. HSBC expects to book a loss of less than $100 million on the sale but absorb around $300 million in restructuring costs as the rest of its Australian retail operation winds down over 18 months.

Blackstone's calculus is the mirror image. Operating outside the banking regulatory perimeter, it faces none of the capital adequacy constraints that make thin mortgage margins punishing for a chartered bank. Inside a private credit fund, those same returns look attractive — especially when Blackstone can pair them with insurance capital through its BXCI arm and expand its Asia-Pacific footprint in one move. Non-bank servicer Pepper Money will manage the book on Blackstone's behalf after closing.

The deal is a vivid data point in a structural shift that has been building for a decade: regulated banks are voluntarily shrinking their balance sheets, and shadow banks are absorbing the slack. Australian borrowers will wake up one morning with a Blackstone-owned mortgage serviced by a non-bank, having never changed their repayment terms. The systemic question — what happens to this credit in the next downturn, with no lender-of-last-resort backstop — remains unanswered.
stories.hook: The bank that used to hold your mortgage for thirty years just sold it to a private equity fund — and that's becoming the new normal.
